analysis.one_liner: Re-regulates basic cable rates, requires cable to carry local TV channels, and caps one company's share of cable subscribers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill in July 1990, but the Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: After Congress deregulated cable rates in 1984, monthly cable bills rose far faster than inflation while most customers had only one cable company to choose from. This bill would have let local authorities cap rates for basic cable where no real competition exists, required cable systems to carry local broadcast and public-television stations, made cable companies sell their programming fairly to satellite and other rivals, and barred any one company from controlling more than 15% of the nation's cable subscribers.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, especially the roughly 56% of TV households that subscribed, would gain protection from rate increases in areas without competition. Local broadcast stations would get guaranteed, unpaid carriage on the lowest-priced tier, protecting free over-the-air TV. Public and educational stations would get guaranteed channel positions. Competing video distributors like satellite operators would get fair access to cable-owned programming.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers and local TV stations

how_it_helps.text: The bill's own findings state that after 1984 rate deregulation, average basic cable rates rose 29%, rose 40% or more for 28% of subscribers, and climbed almost three times faster than the Consumer Price Index [S4].

It would restore rate regulation over basic cable service and equipment wherever a cable system faces no effective competition, defined as having multiple competing multichannel providers reaching enough households [S2][S3].

It would require cable systems using the compulsory copyright license to carry local broadcast stations, place them on the lowest-priced tier, protect their channel positions, and bar operators from accepting payment for carriage or from deleting or moving a station's signal without 30 days' notice [S2][S3][S4].
It would guarantee carriage of at least one or two noncommercial educational (public television) stations, nondiscretionary for every system [S2][S4].
It would cap any single cable operator at 15% of all U.S. cable subscribers, with large operators required to divest down to that level within one year of enactment [S2][S4].

It would bar cable-affiliated programmers from discriminating in price, terms, or availability of programming against rival distributors, and bar cable operators from demanding a financial stake in independent programmers as a condition of carriage [S2][S4].

It would strengthen the franchise renewal process so cities must consider competing proposals, weigh the incumbent's service quality and complaint handling, and give subscribers a voice in the proceeding [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators and their affiliated program networks bear the cost: rates on the basic tier could be capped in most franchises, they must carry local stations for free on their cheapest tier, they would have to sell shares or systems to stay under the 15% subscriber cap, and they must deal fairly with satellite and other competitors. Those costs could be passed to subscribers through non-basic tiers.

drawbacks.text: Must-carry would consume up to one-third of the activated channels of a large cable system, space that could otherwise carry cable networks or new services [S4].

Rate regulation of the basic tier in the roughly 97% of franchises deregulated since 1986 reverses rules cable operators had operated under for years, and caps can reduce the revenue operators have for upgrades and expansion [S4].

Cable operators and the industry argued that re-regulation and the 15% ownership cap would discourage investment and limit economies of scale in a capital-intensive business; the bill also limits the damages cable operators could win from cities in First Amendment lawsuits, which operators saw as an unfair shield for local governments [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For subscribers in the large majority of communities with only one cable company, the bill offered direct rate relief and guaranteed local channels, and the costs fell mainly on a highly concentrated, vertically integrated industry that the bill's own findings described as raising prices three times faster than inflation. The strongest honest objection is that rate caps and forced carriage can dampen investment in a fast-changing technology, and the reported version already softened the original bill by routing rate regulation through the FCC rather than local authorities. On balance, the consumer protections and competition provisions outweigh those costs for ordinary viewers.

outcome.mechanism: The Commerce Committee approved it and placed it on the Senate's calendar of bills waiting for floor action, but no one ever brought it up for a vote before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator John Danforth introduced the bill on November 15, 1989 with a bipartisan group of 15 Senate cosponsors, 8 Democrats and 7 Republicans [S1][S4][S5].

The bill's findings recited that since rate deregulation took effect, basic cable rates had risen about 29% on average, risen 40% or more for 28% of subscribers, and grown almost three times faster than the Consumer Price Index [S4].
The Senate Commerce Committee's communications subcommittee held hearings on March 29, 1990 [S6].

On July 19, 1990 the committee reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment; the amended version shifted rate regulation from local franchising authorities to a system run by the FCC, which could delegate authority back to local regulators [S3][S6].

The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 704), where it sat; the Senate never voted on it, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators and their affiliated programmers came out ahead: they kept deregulated rates, faced no must-carry obligations or 15% ownership cap, and kept their advantages over satellite rivals. Subscribers got nothing from this Congress, though Congress revisited cable regulation soon after.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with 15 cosponsors split 8 Democrats and 7 Republicans, and a Democratic chairman reported it from committee; there was no floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would cap basic rates in the many communities without effective competition, force unpaid carriage of local stations on the cheapest tier, and require any operator controlling more than 15% of U.S. subscribers to divest. Operators' pricing power over a captive subscriber base is what the bill targets.

Cable-owned programming companies would have to sell to satellite and other rival distributors on nondiscriminatory terms, ending their ability to use exclusive carriage to box out competitors. This matters to viewers because it determines what channels non-cable services can offer.
Guaranteed free carriage on the lowest-priced basic tier protects free over-the-air local news and public-affairs programming, including for viewers who cannot afford cable.
The bill makes carriage of one or two noncommercial educational stations mandatory and nondiscretionary, guaranteeing public TV reaches cable households.

industries.industry: Home satellite dish (C-band) owners and satellite TV distributors
industries.note: The reported version requires anyone encrypting satellite cable programming to make it available to home satellite viewers, and gives satellite distributors fair access to cable-owned programming.
